technique: letting one plain object carry the feeling
lesson: Today we work on one technique. One ordinary object in a poem can hold the feeling for you, so the poem doesn't have to name the feeling out loud. Watch the boots in this poem. It says "pulling on the stiff boots by the door," and then "the laces cold enough to ache the finger that threads them." The poem never says the man is tired or dutiful. It gives you the cold laces instead, and you feel the effort through them. Later it says "a bag set on a porch." That plain object carries the whole kindness he's doing. This works because a concrete thing you can picture lands harder than a feeling-word like sad or good. You feel it before you can explain it. Try this: pick one object someone touches, and describe it plainly instead of naming the emotion. The second time through, listen for each object and what it makes you feel. Here is the poem.
poem:
A crow somewhere down the valley says the one thing
it knows, and says it twice, and you are already
pulling on the stiff boots by the door, the laces
cold enough to ache the finger that threads them.
Frost has gone to water on the glass. The kettle
ticks toward its own slow heat. You think of her
up the road, the small ache you can mend with
a bag set on a porch, and it steadies you—
how a man is made plainer by what's asked of him.
The gray lifts off the ridge the way breath lifts.
You've driven worse roads for lighter reasons.

Someone out there is better for the trip you made—
get up and be that kind of near again.
